title: Need advice on how to approach 2D sprite animation + performance
author: resetskillpoints
selftext:
Hey folks, looking for advice on how to approach a few things with a game I'm building.

I'm building a 2D, isometric medieval fantasy city builder, similar to SimCity 2000, but with the added element that giants attack your town and eat your citizens. It's a mixture of SimCity, Pharaoh, Attack on Titan, and They Are Billions. 

I'm making it for my own enjoyment and learning, and I'm running into trouble with a few things:

1. Giant animation - right now I've just got a series of static renders of different actions that the giants cycle through as a place holder, but it looks terrible, sort of like stop motion. I've read that some people use 3D models to model each potential angle and action, and then reimport to 2D. But I'm not really sure what the best way to approach this is. 
2. Game Performance as the number of sprites grow, and the number of giants attack, the game is really slowing down. I'd love any thoughts on how to structure the game for better performance as the number of elements increase.
3. Sprite consistency. I've had some success using a sprite design MD file to try to develop consistency around building size, orientation, and colouring, but it's really struggling with walls. Any advice?

  
Mostly using Codex to build this.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
>Game Performance as the number of sprites grow, and the number of giants attack, the game is really slowing down. I'd love any thoughts on how to structure the game for better performance as the number of elements increase.

 You'll need to profile to find out the bottleneck, because optimizing blindly often doesn't produce results as long as the bottle neck isn't addresssed. When optimizing, you usually go from bottleneck to the next, in a loop of profiling->fixing the bottleneck -> rinse and repeat.   
  
There are usually two culprits in your kind of scenario: 

* Too many single textures for the GPU and it constantly rebinds to different textures. On that one, did you already pack everything together in a texture atlas? This is the classic basic optimization move for such projects. This eliminates most of the costly texture rebinds on the GPU. An nice alternative to that, with some quirks, is also to use texture arrays. 
* Too many instances of enemies for the CPU. For this one, people usually pivot to a non-object oriented style, like a data oriented design. The classic here is the Entity Component System pattern. The main idea is that you stop dealing with single instantiated objects each performing their own behavior, and instead define all entities in bulk in a nicely packed memory layout (e.g. an Array), and then have systems with a single responsibility processing them in bulk each time (e.g. on each frame or each few frames, for example). This makes full use of CPU cache and heavily reduces slow memory accesses.
